questions.question:
When can Product Backlog Refinement occur?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only during Sprint Planning.
choices.explanation: Refinement is not limited to Sprint Planning; it is an ongoing activity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anytime during the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity that can happen at any time during the Sprint.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only during Refinement meetings planned by the Product Owner.
choices.explanation: Refinement does not require formal meetings planned by the Product Owner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Before Sprint Planning.
choices.explanation: Refinement is not a phase before Sprint Planning; it happens continuously.

questions.question:
What would NOT be considered Refactoring?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reordering method parameters to improve readability.
choices.explanation: Reordering parameters to improve readability changes internal structure, which is refactoring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extracting interfaces.
choices.explanation: Extracting interfaces restructures code without changing behavior, which is refactoring.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Renaming things to be more logical.
choices.explanation: Renaming for clarity is a classic refactoring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Changing external interfaces or APIs.
choices.explanation: Changing external interfaces or APIs changes observable behavior for clients; refactoring preserves external behavior.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extracting methods.
choices.explanation: Extracting methods is a classic refactoring.

questions.question:
Your Scrum Team is one of seven teams working on a Software Product. All teams use the same Version Control System. Which is the best approach to deliver a high-quality Increment?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Developers should perform a combination of local and private builds.
choices.explanation: Local and private builds do not ensure that the work of all teams integrates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each team's automated build is integrated toward the end of the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Integrating only at the end of the Sprint delays feedback and increases integration risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is one automated and integrated build for all seven teams.
choices.explanation: One automated, integrated build for all teams gives continuous feedback on a single integrated Increment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each team should have its own automated build.
choices.explanation: Separate builds per team hide integration problems until late.

questions.question:
Who creates documentation included with an Increment?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Developers.
choices.explanation: Documentation is part of the work the Developers do to meet the Definition of Done.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increments do not need documentation.
choices.explanation: Documentation can be required by the Definition of Done or by users; Increments are not exempt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Product Owner.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner does not create the documentation of the Increment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Technical Writers.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no Technical Writer role; the Developers do the work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Scrum Master.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not create product documentation.

questions.question:
What is a merge in a Version Control System?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copying a portion of a code base to isolate it from the original codebase.
choices.explanation: Copying a part of the code base to isolate it is branching, not merging.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Identifying a particular codebase as ready for distribution.
choices.explanation: Marking a code base as ready for distribution is tagging or labelling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Triggering a Deployment into Production.
choices.explanation: Triggering a production deployment is deployment, not merging.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combining two or more versions of code into a single codebase.
choices.explanation: Merging combines two or more versions of code into a single code base.

questions.question:
Which three of the following are feedback loops in Scrum?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily Scrum.
choices.explanation: The Daily Scrum inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the Sprint Backlog.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Release Planning.
choices.explanation: Release Planning is not a Scrum event.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sprint Review.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refinement Meeting.
choices.explanation: Refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal feedback loop event of Scrum.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sprint Retrospective.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective inspects how the Scrum Team works and plans improvements.

questions.question:
Which four types of tests can be included in an automated test harness?
(choose the best four answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Performance.
choices.explanation: Performance tests can be automated and run repeatedly in a harness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exploratory.
choices.explanation: Exploratory testing relies on human investigation and cannot be fully automated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unit.
choices.explanation: Unit tests are the classic automated tests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Functional.
choices.explanation: Functional tests can be automated, for example through the user interface or an API.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Manual regression.
choices.explanation: Manual regression tests are, by definition, not part of an automated harness.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Integration.
choices.explanation: Integration tests can be automated and run in the harness.

questions.question:
Which concept is described by the Last Responsible Moment?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Making decisions as soon as possible to close feedback loops as soon as possible.
choices.explanation: Deciding as soon as possible removes options while uncertainty is still high.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discover decisions to be made as soon as possible but postpone deciding to the latest reasonable moment.
choices.explanation: The Last Responsible Moment means identifying decisions early but deferring them until the cost of not deciding becomes greater than the cost of deciding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The last moment in a Sprint when code changes are allowed, after this only stabilization work should be conducted.
choices.explanation: There is no code freeze moment in a Sprint; quality work continues throughout.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opening a learning window to validate hypotheses and create learning.
choices.explanation: This describes experimentation in general, not the Last Responsible Moment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The last moment a Developer is responsible for quality, after this the Tester is responsible.
choices.explanation: Developers are responsible for quality at all times; there is no hand-off to testers.

questions.question:
Why does a test written using TDD (Test Driven Development) initially fail?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the test has not been refactored.
choices.explanation: Refactoring happens after the test passes, not before it can pass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because it has to be put into an automated test harness to be run.
choices.explanation: A test fails for a functional reason, not because it is not yet in a harness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the tests are checked in before the Product code exists.
choices.explanation: Checking in is not the reason; the test fails because the behavior is not implemented.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the Product code to satisfy the test does not yet exist.
choices.explanation: In TDD the test is written first, so it fails until the product code that satisfies it exists.

questions.question:
When do the Developers show their work to the Product Owner?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever the Product Owner asks.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner can ask to see the work at any time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the Sprint Review.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review is one opportunity, but not the only one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anytime the Developers need feedback from the Product Owner.
choices.explanation: Developers can seek feedback from the Product Owner whenever they need it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All of the above.
choices.explanation: Developers and the Product Owner collaborate continuously; all these situations are valid.

questions.question:
Who decides the System Architecture of a Product developed using Scrum?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Architect chosen by the Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no architect role; the Developers decide.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Software Architect assigned to the Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no assigned Software Architect; architecture is the Developers' responsibility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Developers with input from the Scrum Team and others.
choices.explanation: The Developers decide the architecture, with input from the Scrum Team and others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chief Architect.
choices.explanation: A Chief Architect outside the team does not decide; the Developers do.

questions.question:
When using Continuous Integration, how often should the build be executed?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Once per hour.
choices.explanation: A fixed hourly schedule delays feedback between check-ins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever new or changed code is checked into version control.
choices.explanation: With Continuous Integration, every check-in triggers a build so problems are detected immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Once per day.
choices.explanation: Daily builds are nightly builds, not Continuous Integration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Before the end of the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Building only at the end of the Sprint defeats the purpose of continuous integration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever new tests are created or uncertainty arises about whether old tests will pass.
choices.explanation: The build runs on every change, not only when tests are created or doubts arise.

questions.question:
Who determines how work is performed during the Sprint?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Master.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not decide how the work is done.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Team is self-managing, but the Developers specifically decide how to turn Product Backlog items into an Increment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Team Manager.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no Team Manager.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subject matter experts.
choices.explanation: Experts may advise, but they do not decide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Developers.
choices.explanation: The Developers decide how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

questions.question:
Who creates tests on a Scrum Team?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Product Owner.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner does not create the tests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Developers.
choices.explanation: Testing is part of the Developers' work; they create the tests.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quality Assurance Specialists.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no separate QA role; quality is the Developers' responsibility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Scrum Master.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not create tests.

questions.question:
What is Test First Development (TFD)?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creating tests before satisfying them.
choices.explanation: Test First Development means writing a test before writing the code that satisfies it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Testing existing code before adding more code to it.
choices.explanation: Testing existing code before adding more code is regression testing, not TFD.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Having the Tester in the Scrum Team write the test plans before coding.
choices.explanation: TFD is about executable tests written by Developers, not test plans written by a Tester.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The continuous restructuring of Software to retain flexibility.
choices.explanation: Continuous restructuring of code is refactoring.

questions.question:
Which is the most reliable form of technical documentation?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spreadsheet of passing manual tests.
choices.explanation: Manual test results in a spreadsheet quickly become outdated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Developer's whiteboard.
choices.explanation: A whiteboard is temporary and not reliable documentation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: UML model.
choices.explanation: UML models tend to diverge from the code over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release notes.
choices.explanation: Release notes describe changes, not the system behavior in detail.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A help file.
choices.explanation: Help files are user documentation and may become outdated.

choices.label: F
choices.text: A passing test harness with clear naming and vocabulary.
choices.explanation: Passing tests with clear naming are executable documentation, always in sync with the code.

questions.question:
Who has the final decision about the order of items in the Product Backlog?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Master.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master helps the Product Owner but does not decide the order.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Stakeholders.
choices.explanation: Stakeholders influence the Product Owner, but they do not decide the order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Team contributes to refinement, but the final say on ordering belongs to the Product Owner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Developers.
choices.explanation: Developers can be asked to help, but the Product Owner remains accountable for the order.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Product Owner.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management, including ordering; the organization must respect their decisions.

questions.question:
What are two differences between Unit Tests and Integration Tests?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Unit Test isolates a specific system behavior.
choices.explanation: A unit test isolates a specific behavior of a small unit of code.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An Integration Test usually focuses on the integration of two or more units.
choices.explanation: Integration tests check how two or more units work together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A Unit Test is automated.
choices.explanation: Both kinds of tests can be automated; it is not a difference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An Integration Test runs overnight.
choices.explanation: When a test runs is not what distinguishes it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A Unit Test only runs on a Developer's workstation.
choices.explanation: Unit tests run on build servers too, not only on workstations.

questions.question:
What are the typical roles when practicing Pair Programming?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Product Owner and Developer.
choices.explanation: Pair programming is between Developers, not with the Product Owner.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Business Analyst and Developer.
choices.explanation: Business Analyst is not a pair programming role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tester and Developer.
choices.explanation: Pair programming roles are not job titles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Driver and Navigator.
choices.explanation: In pair programming, the driver writes the code while the navigator reviews and thinks ahead.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Frontend and Backend.
choices.explanation: Frontend and backend are skills, not pair programming roles.

questions.question: True or False: When multiple teams work together on the same Product, each team should maintain a separate Product Backlog.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Multiple teams on one product share one Product Backlog.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: A single product has a single Product Backlog.

questions.question:
What are three of the best ways to address non-functional requirements?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scrum is for functional, front-end development only.
choices.explanation: Scrum applies to all kinds of work, including non-functional requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Important, recurring non-functional requirements can be added to the Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: Recurring non-functional requirements can be part of the Definition of Done, so they apply to every Increment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discuss them during a risk mitigation phase before development.
choices.explanation: There is no separate risk mitigation phase in Scrum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Include them in the Product Backlog.
choices.explanation: Non-functional requirements can be Product Backlog items.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specific expectations can be used as Acceptance Criteria to specific Product Backlog Items.
choices.explanation: Specific expectations can become acceptance criteria of the relevant Product Backlog items.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Before the release, they should be tested and validated in a hardening Sprint.
choices.explanation: There are no hardening Sprints in Scrum; quality is built in every Sprint.

questions.question:
What is the primary purpose of Refactoring?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ensuring that all factors are constantly aligned.
choices.explanation: This is not what refactoring means.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Removing all bugs that were found during Regression Tests.
choices.explanation: Refactoring is not bug fixing; it preserves behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making sure that the code is readable and maintainable.
choices.explanation: Refactoring improves the internal structure of code so it is readable and maintainable, without changing its behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creating better technical documentation.
choices.explanation: Better documentation is not the primary purpose of refactoring.

questions.question:
Which are four attributes of a good bug report?
(choose the best four answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expected results and observed results.
choices.explanation: Comparing expected and observed results makes the problem clear.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Includes build or version number where bug was found.
choices.explanation: The build or version number helps reproduce the bug in the right context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Includes code for a proposed fix.
choices.explanation: A proposed fix is not part of a bug report; the bug report describes the problem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provides simple and repeatable reproduction steps.
choices.explanation: Simple, repeatable reproduction steps are essential to investigate the bug.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Screenshots or other pictures of the bug in action.
choices.explanation: Screenshots help understand the problem, especially in a user interface.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Explains some new system functionality desired.
choices.explanation: New functionality is a feature request, not a bug report.

questions.question:
The practice of decomposing a requirement into failing tests is called:
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Regression Testing.
choices.explanation: Regression testing checks that existing behavior still works.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Object oriented requirements definition.
choices.explanation: This is not an established practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acceptance Test Driven Development.
choices.explanation: Acceptance Test Driven Development expresses requirements as acceptance tests that initially fail.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Behavior Driven Development.
choices.explanation: BDD focuses on behavior described in a shared language; decomposing requirements into failing acceptance tests is ATDD.

questions.question:
What is a mock object?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A test object that mimics the behavior of a dependency in the system under test.
choices.explanation: A mock object imitates a dependency so the system under test can be tested in isolation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mock helps you create a build script.
choices.explanation: Mocks are not related to build scripts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mocks, stubs, dummies, fakes, and shims are all the same.
choices.explanation: Mocks, stubs, fakes and others are different kinds of test doubles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A mock is a way to initialize the database for testing.
choices.explanation: Initializing a database is test setup, not a mock.

questions.question:
Which four are benefits of Test Driven Development?
(choose the best four answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It improves quality and reduces bugs.
choices.explanation: Writing tests first and continuously improves quality and reduces bugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reduces the cost of maintenance over time.
choices.explanation: A good test suite makes changes safer and cheaper over time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It promotes good design and separation of concerns.
choices.explanation: Writing tests first pushes towards small, decoupled, testable designs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It ensures no defects are present in the code.
choices.explanation: No practice can guarantee that code has no defects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It causes you to construct a test harness that can be automated.
choices.explanation: TDD naturally produces an automated test harness.

questions.question:
When using Scrum, can a Scrum Team use Continuous Delivery?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, there is nothing in Scrum that conflicts with Continuous Delivery.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not prevent releasing more often than once per Sprint; Continuous Delivery fits well with Scrum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the Product Owner may not be available each time a PBI is done and the Product Owner has to decide if it should be released.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner can decide release policies; availability is not a reason to forbid Continuous Delivery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because the increment has to be approved at the Sprint Review before it can be released, and a 2-week Sprint would not be considered continuous.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review is not an approval gate; Increments can be released before it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because Stakeholders may have already seen the new features and the Sprint Review will be meaningless.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome and adapts; it stays meaningful even if features are already released.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No, because before releasing an Increment it first has to fulfill the Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: Meeting the Definition of Done is required, and Continuous Delivery is compatible with it.

questions.question:
You are asked to refactor part of the codebase for Application X. When you are done, all Unit Tests pass with 50% Code Coverage. What can you infer from this?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least 50% of Application X functions correctly.
choices.explanation: Coverage does not say how much of the application works correctly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At most 50% of Application X functions correctly.
choices.explanation: Coverage does not give an upper bound on correctness either.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are no bugs present in Application X.
choices.explanation: Passing tests never prove the absence of bugs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: You did not break any existing Unit Tests.
choices.explanation: The only thing you can infer is that your changes did not break the existing unit tests.

questions.question:
What are two ways that regulatory compliance issues are dealt with in Scrum?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are addressed by a separate team who is responsible for compliance issues.
choices.explanation: Compliance is the Scrum Team's responsibility, not a separate team's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are addressed along with functional development of the Product.
choices.explanation: Compliance is addressed along with development, not as an upfront phase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are discussed, determined, and documented before the actual feature development Sprints.
choices.explanation: There is no upfront documentation phase; work emerges.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are added to the Product Backlog and addressed in early Sprints, while always requiring at least some business functionality. no matter how small.
choices.explanation: Compliance items can be in the Product Backlog and addressed in early Sprints, always alongside business functionality.

questions.question: True or False: User Stories are required in the Product Backlog.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not prescribe User Stories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: User Stories are an optional practice; Product Backlog items can take any form.

questions.question:
In Software Development, DRY refers to:
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Code with low Cyclomatic Complexity.
choices.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity is another metric.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Code with minimal duplication.
choices.explanation: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) means avoiding duplication of knowledge in code.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Code that has not been peer reviewed.
choices.explanation: Peer review is not what DRY means.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Code that has been peer reviewed.
choices.explanation: Peer review is not what DRY means.

questions.question:
Which statements are true when multiple Scrum Teams work on a Software Product at the same time?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: All Scrum Teams work in their own version control branch.
choices.explanation: Long-lived separate branches delay integration and hide problems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Code is merged at the Scrum of Scrums.
choices.explanation: Scrum of Scrums is not a merge step; integration must be continuous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Scrum Teams must integrate their work before the end of the Sprint.
choices.explanation: All teams must integrate their work into a single Increment before the end of the Sprint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Scrum Teams coordinate their work to deliver a single Increment.
choices.explanation: The teams coordinate to deliver one integrated Increment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each Scrum Team should have a different Product Owner.
choices.explanation: A product has one Product Owner, whatever the number of teams.

questions.question:
Which answer best describes Behavior Driven Development (BDD)?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A style of Test Driven Development focusing on user and system interactions.
choices.explanation: BDD is a style of TDD that describes system behavior from the user's point of view.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A development style that accounts for leadership style among team members.
choices.explanation: BDD is not about leadership styles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A way to organize Unit Tests based on class and method structures.
choices.explanation: BDD focuses on behavior, not on code structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A technique for maintaining Regression Test harnesses.
choices.explanation: BDD is not a technique for maintaining regression tests.

questions.question:
In what ways do Developers contribute to refining the Product Backlog?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: They ask questions in order to clarify the intent of Product Backlog Items.
choices.explanation: Developers ask questions to understand the intent of Product Backlog items.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They do not. The Developers are only responsible for prioritizing technical work.
choices.explanation: Developers contribute to refinement; ordering is the Product Owner's accountability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They do not. The Scrum Master and the Product Owner are responsible for Product Backlog Refinement.
choices.explanation: Refinement involves the whole Scrum Team, especially the Developers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They give input on technical dependencies.
choices.explanation: Developers share technical dependencies and constraints.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They may update estimates for Product Backlog Items.
choices.explanation: The Developers size the items and can update their estimates.

questions.question:
When should the Developers create their first automated build?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Just before the Product is released.
choices.explanation: Automating the build only before release removes all early feedback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before writing the first line of code.
choices.explanation: Without code there is nothing to build yet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the Product Owner asks for a build.
choices.explanation: The build should not depend on a request from the Product Owner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Just before the end of the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Waiting until the end of the Sprint delays feedback.

choices.label: E
choices.text: As soon as there is code in the Version Control System.
choices.explanation: As soon as code exists in version control, it should be built automatically.

questions.question:
Why might Developers choose to do Pair Programming?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Information sharing and learning.
choices.explanation: Pairing spreads knowledge and helps learning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Improving Code Quality.
choices.explanation: Continuous review while coding improves quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Efficiency.
choices.explanation: Fewer defects and shared understanding can make the team more efficient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can be a fun way to work.
choices.explanation: Many people enjoy working in pairs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All of the above.
choices.explanation: All these are valid reasons to pair.

questions.question:
What is the role of Modeling in Scrum Teams?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Models are not used by agile teams.
choices.explanation: Models are used by agile teams when they help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Models are maintained along with the Software as it emerges.
choices.explanation: Models do not have to be maintained; they are often temporary communication tools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Models are assembly instructions for the Developers.
choices.explanation: Models are not detailed instructions; Developers decide how to build.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modeling may be useful to increase shared understanding.
choices.explanation: Modeling helps build a shared understanding of the problem or the design.

questions.question:
Which of the following are DevOps Practices?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment / Continuous Delivery.
choices.explanation: CI/CD practices are core DevOps practices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blue-Green Deployment.
choices.explanation: Blue-green deployment is a DevOps deployment practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypothesis Driven Development.
choices.explanation: Hypothesis-driven development is part of the DevOps culture of experimentation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vertical Teams.
choices.explanation: Teams organized around value streams are a DevOps practice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blameless Postmortem.
choices.explanation: Blameless postmortems support learning, a DevOps practice.

choices.label: F
choices.text: All of the above.
choices.explanation: All of these are DevOps practices.

questions.question:
While practicing Test Driven Development, what is done after the test fails?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Write the minimum amount of Product code to satisfy the test.
choices.explanation: Write just enough production code to make the failing test pass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Refactor the test so the code passes.
choices.explanation: The test is not changed to pass; the code is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run it again to make sure it really fails.
choices.explanation: Running it again does not help; the next step is to make it pass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Implement the required functionality.
choices.explanation: TDD implements in small steps, not the whole functionality at once.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Meet with the Business Analyst to ensure that the test is correct.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no Business Analyst role; the test expresses the expected behavior.

questions.question:
What tactic should a Scrum Master use to divide a group of 100 people into multiple Scrum Teams?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create teams based on their skills across multiple layers (such as database, UI, etc.).
choices.explanation: Deciding for people goes against self-management.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ask the people to divide themselves into teams.
choices.explanation: Letting people self-organize into teams fosters ownership and self-management.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ask the Product Owner to assign the people to teams.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner does not assign people to teams.

questions.question:
What is an Integration Test?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A test of the user interface.
choices.explanation: User interface tests are a different category.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A test runs during a Continuous Integration build.
choices.explanation: Any test can run during a CI build; that does not define an integration test.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A test of a single unit of functionality.
choices.explanation: A test of a single unit is a unit test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A test of multiple units of functionality.
choices.explanation: An integration test checks several units working together.

questions.question:
Which of the following describes the focus of the first way of DevOps?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first set of practices a team should apply before moving to the second way.
choices.explanation: The three ways are principles, not a sequence of practice sets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Using automated build and release pipelines.
choices.explanation: Pipelines are a means; the first way focuses on flow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To deliver value earlier and more frequently.
choices.explanation: The first way is about flow: delivering value from development to operations earlier and more often.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tool-focused way of introducing DevOps, compared to a mindset way (second way) and organizational structure (third way).
choices.explanation: The ways are not a tool, mindset and organization classification.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A culture of continuous experimentation and learning.
choices.explanation: Continuous experimentation and learning is the third way.

questions.question:
Which of the following is true about the Definition of Done?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It might be a subject of discussion during Sprint Retrospective.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done can be inspected and improved during the Sprint Retrospective.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the sole responsibility of the Developers to define it.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done is created by the Scrum Team, or follows an organizational standard.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is synonymous with Acceptance Criteria.
choices.explanation: Acceptance criteria are specific to an item; the Definition of Done applies to all work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can only be extended; nothing can be removed.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done can evolve in both directions, even though it usually gets stronger.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It defines a state when the entire Increment is releasable.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done describes the state of a releasable Increment.

questions.question:
At Sprint Planning, the Scrum Team has NO clear standard to meet for releasable Software. What should the Scrum Team do?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask the Product Owner to specify a Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done belongs to the Scrum Team, not the Product Owner alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a unique completion checklist for each item in the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Separate checklists per item do not create a shared quality standard.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify a shared Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: If there is no organizational standard, the Scrum Team creates a shared Definition of Done.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ask the Scrum Master what they should do.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not decide; the Scrum Team does.

questions.question: True or False: Database design must be complete before coding starts to ensure a solid foundation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Design emerges; a complete database design upfront is not required.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: The database design can emerge with the functionality, sprint after sprint.

questions.question:
The Daily Scrum event happens every day. What would be three concerns if the frequency were to be lowered to every two to three days?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opportunities to inspect and adapt in the Sprint Backlog are lost.
choices.explanation: The Daily Scrum exists to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog. Reducing its frequency reduces inspection and adaptation opportunities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Master loses the ability to update the Gantt Chart properly.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not require a Gantt chart, and updating one is not tied to the Daily Scrum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Too much work is spent updating the Scrum Board before meeting.
choices.explanation: Updating the Scrum board is not the purpose of the Daily Scrum. Lowering the frequency does not directly create extra work for board updates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sprint Plan may become inaccurate.
choices.explanation: Without daily inspection, the Sprint Backlog may not reflect current progress or remaining work, leading to inaccuracies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impediments are raised and resolved more slowly.
choices.explanation: The Daily Scrum helps surface impediments quickly. Meeting less often delays identifying and addressing them.

choices.label: F
choices.text: The Product Owner cannot accurately report to the Stakeholders.
choices.explanation: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal. It is not primarily for enabling stakeholder reporting.

questions.question:
Which of the following are required by Scrum?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release Burnup Chart.
choices.explanation: Burnup charts are optional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Burndown Chart.
choices.explanation: Burndown charts are optional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unit Tests.
choices.explanation: Unit tests are good practice but not required by Scrum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critical Path Analysis.
choices.explanation: Critical path analysis is not part of Scrum.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Refactoring.
choices.explanation: Refactoring is a good practice, not a Scrum requirement.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Build automation.
choices.explanation: Build automation is good practice, not required by Scrum.

choices.label: G
choices.text: None of the above.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not require any of these practices.

questions.question:
Which of the following best describes Emergent Architecture?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Starting development of a Software Product requires a clear understanding of the underlying Software Architecture and Emergent Architecture describes the process of creating this initial architecture.
choices.explanation: Emergent architecture is the opposite of a fully defined upfront architecture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Software Architecture emerges solely decisions the Developers make from a technical perspective.
choices.explanation: Architecture is not only technical; business needs shape it as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In Scrum there is no Architecture-Role therefore architecture emerges naturally.
choices.explanation: Architecture does not emerge by chance; the Developers deliberately evolve it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The desire to make decisions easier to change in the future and find the best possible point in time to make decisions.
choices.explanation: Emergent architecture keeps decisions easy to change and takes them at the most appropriate moment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enterprise Architects must be involved to create the foundation of each Software Product.
choices.explanation: Architecture is the Developers' responsibility, not set upfront by enterprise architects.

questions.question:
Which are two benefits of establishing naming conventions for code?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: To make it easy to distinguish between different Software Products.
choices.explanation: Naming conventions are about code, not product identification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To make the code more readable.
choices.explanation: Consistent names make the code easier to read.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To communicate the identity of the Developer who worked on the code.
choices.explanation: Authorship is tracked by version control, not by names in the code.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To reduce friction in a shared codebase.
choices.explanation: Shared conventions reduce friction when many people work on the same code.

choices.label: E
choices.text: To ensure that abandoned functions are not created.
choices.explanation: Naming conventions do not prevent dead code.

questions.question:
Does delivering changes frequently and directly into Production help to reduce risk?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because the changes you make are much smaller and it is easier to fix problems.
choices.explanation: Small changes are easier to understand, test and fix if something goes wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because each release means a risk to break something so releasing more frequently would increase the risk.
choices.explanation: Frequent releases are smaller, so each one carries less risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because frequent release encourage the Developers to automate the release process.
choices.explanation: Automation is a consequence, not the reason why risk is reduced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because you get earlier feedback and can learn faster.
choices.explanation: Frequent releases bring earlier feedback, so problems and wrong assumptions are found sooner.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No, the only way to tackle these risks is by extensive risk management.
choices.explanation: Heavy risk management is not the only answer; small, frequent releases reduce risk.

choices.label: F
choices.text: No, because releasing needs extensive testing which cannot be conducted frequently.
choices.explanation: Testing can be automated so it runs on every release.

questions.question: True or False: Best Practices are recommended to solve complex problems.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Complex problems have no single best practice; they require experimentation and empiricism.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Best practices suit simple problems; complex problems need emergent practices discovered empirically.

questions.question:
When is Performance Testing most effectively performed?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Often, throughout development of the Software.
choices.explanation: Performance should be tested continuously, so problems are found early when they are cheap to fix.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Just before deploying to Production.
choices.explanation: Waiting until just before production finds problems too late.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After coding is complete.
choices.explanation: Coding is never really complete; testing late delays feedback.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In Production.
choices.explanation: Production monitoring helps, but performance testing should happen well before.

questions.question:
Which three of the following criteria are most helpful as part of a Scrum Team's Definition of Done?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Product is released at the end of every Sprint.
choices.explanation: Releasing is a Product Owner decision, not a Definition of Done criterion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acceptance Tests pass.
choices.explanation: Passing acceptance tests show that items meet their acceptance criteria.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Code Review is done.
choices.explanation: Code reviews help maintain quality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regression Tests pass.
choices.explanation: Passing regression tests ensure existing functionality still works.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No impediments exist.
choices.explanation: The absence of impediments is not a quality criterion.

questions.question:
A team has expressed requirements as a set of failing Acceptance Tests. What are two benefits?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improves quality in the requirement itself.
choices.explanation: Writing requirements as tests forces them to be precise, which improves the requirement itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear Acceptance Criteria for each feature.
choices.explanation: Each feature gets clear, executable acceptance criteria.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Using a code generation tool, the solution can be generated from the requirements model.
choices.explanation: Acceptance tests do not generate the solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promotes the use of DRY principle.
choices.explanation: Acceptance tests are not specifically related to DRY.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tracking of competencies.
choices.explanation: Acceptance tests do not track competencies.

questions.question:
Which is LEAST useful when measuring Code Maintainability?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Function Points.
choices.explanation: Function points measure functional size, not maintainability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclomatic Complexity.
choices.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity indicates how hard code is to understand and test.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depth of Inheritance.
choices.explanation: Depth of inheritance indicates structural complexity, relevant to maintainability.

questions.question:
Which two criteria are useful in deciding if something should be documented every Sprint?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Master requires it.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not decide what is documented.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is required by the Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: If the Definition of Done requires documentation, it is done every Sprint.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The documentation is used to enhance and maintain the Software.
choices.explanation: Documentation that actually helps to evolve and maintain the software is worth producing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Software tool being used requires it.
choices.explanation: A tool's requirements are not a good reason to document.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It has always been documented in the past.
choices.explanation: Tradition alone is not a good reason to document.

questions.question:
Which of the following are quality goals in Application Architecture?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Build.
choices.explanation: Build is a process, not a quality goal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Security.
choices.explanation: Security is a quality attribute of an architecture.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Design Pattern selection.
choices.explanation: Design patterns are means, not quality goals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scalability.
choices.explanation: Scalability is a quality attribute of an architecture.

questions.question: True or False: Stakeholders can be included in Product Backlog Refinement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Stakeholders can help clarify items during refinement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Refinement is open to anyone who can help; stakeholders may be included.

questions.question:
You are the Scrum Master on a newly formed Scrum Team. Which two of the following activities would probably help the team in starting up?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ensure the Scrum Team members have compatible personalities.
choices.explanation: Personality compatibility is not something the Scrum Master ensures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introduce a bonus system for the top performers in the team.
choices.explanation: Individual bonuses undermine team collaboration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ensure the team understands they need a Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: A Definition of Done is needed to create Done Increments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have the development managers for each Developer introduce their direct reports and go over their responsibilities on the Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: Managers presenting their staff undermine self-management.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ask the Product Owner to discuss the Product, its vision, history, goals, and context, as well as answer questions.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner shares context and goals so the team understands the product.

questions.question:
Which best describes the Product Backlog?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains all foreseeable tasks and requirements from which the Scrum team can develop and maintain a complete project plan.
choices.explanation: The Product Backlog is never complete.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is allowed to grow and change as more is learned about the Product and its customers.
choices.explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent; it grows and changes as more is learned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is baselined to follow change management processes.
choices.explanation: The Product Backlog is never baselined.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides just enough information to enable a Scrum team to start the design phase of a Product.
choices.explanation: There is no design phase in Scrum.

questions.question:
What are two responsibilities of Testers among the Developers?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Verifying the work of programmers.
choices.explanation: There is no role checking other people's work; Developers are collectively accountable for quality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scrum has no "Tester" role.
choices.explanation: Scrum only recognizes Developers, the Product Owner and the Scrum Master; there are no Testers as a role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Finding bugs.
choices.explanation: Finding bugs is part of the Developers' work, not a separate role in Scrum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every Developer is responsible for quality.
choices.explanation: The Developers are accountable for instilling quality by adhering to the Definition of Done.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tracking quality metrics.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not define specialised roles like Tester; quality is the responsibility of the Developers.

questions.question:
For the purpose of transparency, when does Scrum say a new Increment of working Software must be available?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the Product Owner asks to create one.
choices.explanation: Creating Increments is not on request; it happens every Sprint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At the end of every Sprint.
choices.explanation: At least one useful Increment is created every Sprint; it may be delivered even earlier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before the release Sprint.
choices.explanation: Release Sprints do not exist in Scrum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every 3 Sprints.
choices.explanation: An Increment must be available every Sprint, not every three Sprints.

choices.label: E
choices.text: After the Acceptance Testing phase.
choices.explanation: There is no separate acceptance testing phase in Scrum.

questions.question:
Which three behaviors demonstrate that a team is self-managing?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Developers inviting external people to the Sprint Planning to ask them how to turn a Product Backlog Item into an Increment via a complete and detailed Sprint Backlog.
choices.explanation: Asking outsiders how to do the work shows a lack of self-management.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Developers are working within the boundaries of their functional description and nicely handing off work from analyst to Developer to Tester to integration.
choices.explanation: Hand-offs between functional roles show the team is not cross-functional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Product Owner doesn't need to be at Sprint Retrospectives.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner is a Scrum Team member and participates in the Retrospective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stakeholders walking in at the Daily Scrum to check progress and work with the Scrum Master to optimize the functional scope for the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Stakeholders steering the Sprint at the Daily Scrum undermines self-management.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Developers collaboratively selecting their own work during the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Collaboratively selecting their own work shows self-management.

choices.label: F
choices.text: The Scrum Master is no longer needed.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master is always part of a Scrum Team.

choices.label: G
choices.text: The Developers have all the skills needed to create a releasable Increment.
choices.explanation: Having all the necessary skills shows a cross-functional, self-managing team.

choices.label: H
choices.text: The Developers creating their own Sprint Backlog, reflecting all work that is part of the Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: Creating their own Sprint Backlog with all the work needed for Done shows self-management.

questions.question:
What is the purpose of a Sprint Review?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: To take time to judge the validity of the project.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review is not about judging the project.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To inspect the Product Increment with the Stakeholders and collect feedback on next steps.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the Sprint with stakeholders and determines future adaptations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To review the Scrum Team's activities and processes during the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Reviewing the team's processes is the Sprint Retrospective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To build team spirit.
choices.explanation: Team building is not its purpose.

questions.question:
Which statement best describes the Sprint Backlog as outcome of the Sprint Planning?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the Developers plan for the Sprint.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every item has a designated owner.
choices.explanation: Items are not assigned to individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a complete list of all work to be done in a Sprint.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Backlog emerges; it is not complete at Sprint Planning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each task is estimated in hours.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not require tasks or hour estimates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is ordered by the Product Owner.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, not the Sprint Backlog.

questions.question:
The Developers select a set of Product Backlog Items for a Sprint Backlog with the intent to get the selected items "Done" by the end of the Sprint. Which three phrases best describe the purpose of a Definition of Done?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It provides a template for elements that need to be included in the technical documentation.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done is not a documentation template.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guides the Developers in creating a forecast at the Sprint Planning.
choices.explanation: Knowing what Done means helps the Developers estimate how much work they can take into the Sprint.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It controls whether the Developers have performed their tasks.
choices.explanation: It is not a control tool over individuals; Developers are self-managing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It creates transparency over the work inspected at the Sprint Review.
choices.explanation: It creates transparency by giving everyone a shared understanding of what was completed and is inspected at the Sprint Review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It defines what it takes for an Increment to be ready for release.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done describes the quality required for the Increment to be usable and releasable.

choices.label: F
choices.text: It tracks the percentage complete of a Product Backlog Item.
choices.explanation: Done is binary; the Definition of Done does not track percentages.

questions.question:
Which output from Sprint Planning provides the Developers with a target and overarching direction for the Sprint?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Sprint Goal.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Goal provides the target and overarching direction for the Sprint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sprint Review minutes.
choices.explanation: Sprint Review minutes are not an output of Sprint Planning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Release Plan.
choices.explanation: A release plan is not an official Scrum output of Sprint Planning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Sprint Backlog.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Backlog contains selected work and a plan, but not the overarching direction itself.

questions.question:
The Product Owner determines how many Product Backlog Items the Developers select for a Sprint.
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: True, but only after confirmation by the resource manager that the Team has enough capacity.
choices.explanation: There is no resource manager deciding capacity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False, capacity and commitment are the Project Manager's responsibility.
choices.explanation: There is no Project Manager in Scrum; the Developers decide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: False, the Scrum Master does that.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not decide; the Developers do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner does not decide how much work the Developers take.

choices.label: E
choices.text: True, accordingly to what was committed to the Stakeholders.
choices.explanation: Stakeholder commitments do not dictate how much the Developers select.

choices.label: F
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Only the Developers decide how much work they select for a Sprint.

questions.question:
Who owns the Sprint Backlog?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: While the Scrum Team collaborates, it is specifically the Developers who decide how many Product Backlog items they select for a Sprint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Master.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master facilitates Scrum events but does not determine the amount of work selected for the Sprint.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Developers.
choices.explanation: The Developers determine how much work they can undertake in a Sprint based on their capacity and Definition of Done.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Product Owner.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog but does not decide how much work Developers can take into a Sprint.

questions.question:
When is implementation of a Product Backlog Item considered complete?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the item has no work remaining in order to be potentially released.
choices.explanation: An item is complete when it meets the Definition of Done, with no work remaining before it could be released.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When Quality Assurance reports that the item passes all Acceptance Criteria.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no separate QA; Done is defined by the Definition of Done.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At the end of the Sprint.
choices.explanation: The end of the Sprint does not make work Done.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When all work in the Sprint Backlog related to the item is finished.
choices.explanation: Finishing the tasks is not enough if the Definition of Done is not met.

questions.question:
Which two of the following are true about the Scrum Master role?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Master teaches the Developers to keep the Scrum meetings to their time-box.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures events are productive and kept within the timebox.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Master is responsible for updating the Sprint Burndown.
choices.explanation: Developers track their own progress; the Scrum Master is not responsible for a burndown.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Scrum Master assigns tasks to Developers when they need work.
choices.explanation: Developers self-manage and pick their own work; the Scrum Master does not assign tasks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Scrum Master helps those outside the team interact with the Scrum Team.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master helps those outside the Scrum Team understand which interactions are helpful.

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the Sprint Review, the Scrum Master identifies what has been "Done" and what has not been "Done".
choices.explanation: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not judged by the Scrum Master at the Sprint Review.

questions.question:
Which two of the following are appropriate topics for discussion during a Sprint Retrospective?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Documenting Acceptance Criteria for items in the next Sprint.
choices.explanation: Acceptance criteria are refined during Product Backlog refinement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The order of items in the Product Backlog.
choices.explanation: Ordering the Product Backlog is for the Product Owner, typically outside the Retrospective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Identifying high priority process improvements for the next Sprint.
choices.explanation: The Retrospective identifies the most helpful process improvements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: How the team collaborates.
choices.explanation: The Retrospective inspects how individuals, interactions and processes worked.

questions.question: True or False: Multiple Scrum Teams working on the same project must have the same Sprint start date.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Teams on the same product do not need the same Sprint start date, as long as they integrate their work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not require the same start date for all teams.

questions.question:
When is it most appropriate for a Scrum Team to change the Definition of Done?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: During Sprint Planning.
choices.explanation: Sprint Planning focuses on selecting and planning work for the Sprint, not on inspecting and adapting the Definition of Done.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prior to starting a new project.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done can evolve as the Scrum Team learns and improves, not only prior to starting a new project.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prior to starting a new Sprint.
choices.explanation: The Definition of Done can evolve as the Scrum Team learns and improves, not only prior to starting a new project.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During the Sprint Retrospective.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is where the Scrum Team inspects how it worked and adapts its practices, which can include improving the Definition of Done.

questions.question:
The Product Owner is not collaborating with the Developers during the Sprint. What are two valuable actions for a Scrum Master to take?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nominate a proxy Product Owner.
choices.explanation: A proxy Product Owner is not part of Scrum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coach the Product Owner in the values of Scrum and incremental delivery.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master coaches the Product Owner on the importance of collaboration and incremental delivery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stop the Sprint, send the Product Owner to a course and restart.
choices.explanation: Stopping the Sprint is not appropriate; only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inform the Product Owner's functional manager.
choices.explanation: Escalating to a manager is not the first step; coaching is.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bring up the problem in the Sprint Retrospective.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is the right moment to discuss collaboration.

questions.question:
A Scrum Master is working with Developers who are in different physical locations. They meet in a variety of meeting rooms and have much to do logistically (for example, set up conference calls) before the Daily Scrum. What action should the Scrum Master take?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask the Developers to alternate who is responsible for meeting setup.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master should not impose a solution, even a rotation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set up the meeting and tell the Developers that is how it will be done.
choices.explanation: Imposing a solution undermines self-management.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inform Management and ask them to solve it.
choices.explanation: Escalating to management for a team issue removes autonomy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow the Developers to self-manage and determine for themselves what to do.
choices.explanation: Developers self-manage and can solve their own logistic problems.

questions.question:
Five new Scrum Teams have been created to build one Product. A few of the Developers on one of the Developers ask the Scrum Master how to coordinate their work with the other teams. What should the Scrum Master do?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teach the Product Owner to work with the Lead Developers on ordering Product Backlog in a way to avoid too much technical and development overlap during a Sprint.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no lead Developers, and ordering does not replace coordination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collect the Sprint tasks from the teams at the end of their Sprint Planning and merge that into a consolidated plan for the entire Sprint.
choices.explanation: Consolidating plans is centralized control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Teach them that it is their responsibility to work with the other teams to create an integrated Increment.
choices.explanation: The Developers are responsible for working with the other teams to create an integrated Increment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visit the five teams each day to inspect that their Sprint Backlogs are aligned.
choices.explanation: Daily inspection by the Scrum Master is control, not coaching.

questions.question: True or False: Scrum is a methodology that tells in detail how to build Software incrementally.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Scrum is a framework, not a detailed methodology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Scrum is intentionally incomplete; it does not tell in detail how to build software.

questions.question:
In the Sprint Planning meeting, the Product Owner and the Developers were unable to reach a clear understanding about the highest order Product Backlog Items. Because of this, the Developers couldn't figure out how many Product Backlog Items it could forecast for the upcoming Sprint. They were able to agree on a Sprint Goal, however. Which of the following two actions should the Scrum Master support?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask everyone to take as much time as needed to analyze the Product Backlog first, and then reconvene another Sprint Planning meeting.
choices.explanation: Postponing planning delays the Sprint; Sprints follow each other without gaps.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cancel the Sprint. Send the entire team to an advanced Scrum training and then start a new Sprint.
choices.explanation: Cancelling the Sprint is not appropriate, and only the Product Owner can cancel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forecast the most likely Product Backlog Items to meet the goal and create a Sprint Backlog based on a likely initial design and plan. Once the time-box for the Sprint Planning meeting is over, start the Sprint and continue to analyze, decompose, and create additional functionality during the Sprint.
choices.explanation: With a Sprint Goal, the Developers can forecast the likely items, start, and refine during the Sprint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Continue the Sprint Planning meeting past its time-box until an adequate number of Product Backlog Items are well enough understood for the Developers to make a complete forecast. Then start the Sprint.
choices.explanation: Sprint Planning is timeboxed; it cannot be extended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Discuss in the upcoming Sprint Retrospective why this happened and what changes will make it less likely to recur.
choices.explanation: The Retrospective is the place to understand why this happened and improve.

questions.question:
A member of the Developers takes the Scrum Master aside to express his concerns about data security issues. What should the Scrum Master do?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a Product Backlog Item for security.
choices.explanation: Creating a Product Backlog item may be an outcome, but the team must first be aware of the issue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ask the person to share the issue with the team as soon as possible.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master encourages transparency and self-management: the team, informed, decides how to address it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add security to the Definition of Done.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not decide alone; the team should first discuss the concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tell the Product Owner to stop further development of features until the issues are fixed.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master does not order the Product Owner to stop development.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Go check with the Testers.
choices.explanation: Scrum has no tester role; quality and security are the Scrum Team's responsibility.

questions.question:
What are two ways that architecture and infrastructure are handled in Scrum?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are implemented along with functional development of the Product.
choices.explanation: Architecture and infrastructure are built along with business functionality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are built by a separate team through the creation of an architectural runway.
choices.explanation: A separate team creating a runway creates dependencies and delays value.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are added to the Product Backlog and addressed in early Sprints, while always requiring at least some business functionality, no matter how small.
choices.explanation: Architecture work can be in the Product Backlog and addressed in early Sprints, always with some business functionality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are discussed, determined, and documented before the actual feature development Sprints.
choices.explanation: There is no upfront phase before feature Sprints.

questions.question:
What are three ways Scrum promotes self-management?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: By preventing Stakeholders from entering the development room.
choices.explanation: Stakeholders are not prevented from interacting with the team.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By removing titles for the Developers.
choices.explanation: Scrum recognizes no titles for Developers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By not allowing documentation.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not forbid documentation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By being a lightweight framework.
choices.explanation: Scrum is lightweight, leaving room for the team to decide how to work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: By the Developers deciding what work to do in a Sprint.
choices.explanation: Developers select the work for the Sprint.

questions.question: True or False: Cross-functional teams are optimized to work on one technical layer of a system only (e.g. GUI, database, middle tier, interfaces).

choices.label: A
choices.text: False.
choices.explanation: Working on a single layer is the opposite of cross-functionality; it creates dependencies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True.
choices.explanation: Cross-functional teams have all skills needed to create value across all layers.

questions.question:
What are three benefits of self-management?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased accuracy of estimates.
choices.explanation: Estimates are not necessarily more accurate; uncertainty remains in complex work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased rule compliance.
choices.explanation: Self-management is not about compliance with rules; it is about autonomy over who does what, when and how.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased self-accountability.
choices.explanation: Self-managing teams own their work and feel more accountable for the outcome.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased creativity.
choices.explanation: Autonomy encourages people to find new and better solutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased commitment.
choices.explanation: People who decide how to do their work are more committed to it.

questions.question:
Why does a Scrum Team need a Sprint Goal?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Sprint Goal ensures that all of the Product Backlog Items selected for the Sprint are implemented.
choices.explanation: Scope can be renegotiated while the Sprint Goal stays; the goal does not guarantee every item is done.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Team is more focused with a common yet specific goal.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Goal creates coherence and focus, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sprint Goals are not valuable. Everything is known from the Product Backlog.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Goal is a commitment of the Sprint Backlog and gives the Sprint a purpose beyond the list of items.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A Sprint Goal only gives purpose to Sprint 0.
choices.explanation: Sprint 0 does not exist in Scrum, and every Sprint has a Sprint Goal.

questions.question:
How should Product Backlog Items be chosen when multiple Scrum Teams work from the same Product Backlog?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Product Owner should provide each team with its own Product Backlog.
choices.explanation: One product has one Product Backlog.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Developers pull in work in agreement with the Product Owner.
choices.explanation: Developers pull work from the shared Product Backlog in agreement with the Product Owner.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each Scrum Team takes an equal numbers of items.
choices.explanation: Equal distribution is arbitrary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Scrum Team with the highest velocity pulls Product Backlog Items first.
choices.explanation: Velocity does not decide who pulls work first.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Product Owner decides.
choices.explanation: The Developers select the work; the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog.

questions.question:
Which of the following describe Test Driven Development?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Software Development technique based on automated tests.
choices.explanation: TDD is a development technique based on automated tests written before the code.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A predictable way to develop working, well-organized code.
choices.explanation: TDD does not make development predictable; it improves feedback and design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Having Testers in the development process.
choices.explanation: TDD is a developer practice; it does not require testers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An incremental and emergent approach to Software Design.
choices.explanation: TDD makes design emerge incrementally, test after test.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Creating a manual test script before writing code.
choices.explanation: TDD uses automated tests, not manual scripts.

questions.question:
What happens during Sprint 0?
(choose the best answer)
